readerTitle: Why the night market recruits cooks before crowds
caseNote: 가상 사례 (야시장, 장부 관리 매칭, 청소 매칭, 사진 작가 앱) + 실제 연구 (쇼핑몰 앵커 임대료) + 실제 기업 (OpenTable)
insight: 마켓플레이스는 돈을 내는 쪽이 아니라 구하기 어려운 쪽, 그리고 있기만 하면 반대편을 끌어오는 쪽부터 만든다.
misconception: 돈을 내는 쪽(구매자)부터 모으면 된다. 또는 마켓플레이스는 언제나 공급자부터 모아야 한다.

sources.text: Gould, E. D., Pashigian, B. P., & Prendergast, C. J. (2005). Contracts, Externalities, and Incentives in Shopping Malls. Review of Economics and Statistics.
Dixon, C. (2015). Come for the tool, stay for the network. cdixon.org
야시장, 장부 관리, 청소, 사진 작가 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Gould 외(2005)가 미국 쇼핑몰에서 앵커 매장이 소형 매장보다 면적당 임대료를 훨씬 적게 낸다고 보고했는지 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 구체적 수치를 넣지 않았습니다.
OpenTable이 초기에 온라인 예약 손님이 없어도 쓸모 있는 예약 관리 소프트웨어로 식당을 먼저 모았다는 내용이 Chris Dixon 에세이에 나오는지 확인하세요.
softwareNote의 앱 플랫폼이 개발자를 먼저 공략한다는 내용은 특정 기업 사실이 아닌 일반적 설명으로 적었습니다.

cards.title: Why the night market recruits cooks before crowds
body: A new weekend night market opens in a parking lot in three months. The organizer has spent almost nothing on posters or ads.
Instead, she has visited 60 food stalls, offering each one its first month free. Shoppers can wait. She's betting they'll come for the stalls.

image.label: Organizer walking past food stalls before opening night
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 저녁 주차장에 노점 천막이 하나둘 세워지고, 클립보드를 든 주최자가 요리사와 악수. 손님은 아직 없고 멀리 빈 공간. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: One push, two sides.
body: You're launching a service that matches small businesses with freelance bookkeepers in one city. Owners say good bookkeepers are hard to find. The best ones are already busy and turn down work.
You have budget for one big push this quarter. Where does it go?

options.text: Ads to small businesses, since they're the ones who pay
options.feedback: Owners arrive, find few good bookkeepers, and leave disappointed. You paid to show them an empty shelf.

options.text: Win 15–20 trusted bookkeepers first, with guaranteed clients or lower fees
options.feedback: You spend on the side that's hard to get. Owners already want bookkeepers, so a strong list gives them a reason to come.

options.text: Split the budget evenly between both sides
options.feedback: It feels balanced, but half the money goes to the side that's easy to attract, and the bookkeeper list may stay too thin to matter.

cards.title: Shopping malls solved this long ago.
body: Malls usually sign a big department store or supermarket first. Real estate people call it the **anchor**.
Economists who studied US malls found that anchors pay far less rent per square foot than small shops. The small shops pay more because they live off the shoppers the anchor brings in.
The landlord isn't being generous. It's paying the side whose presence brings everyone else.

image.label: Mall floor plan with one big anchor store and small shops around it
image.brief: 쇼핑몰 평면도 인포그래픽. 한쪽 끝에 큰 "Anchor" 매장(낮은 임대료 태그), 주변 작은 매장들(높은 임대료 태그). 앵커에서 손님 화살표가 작은 매장으로 흘러감. 실제 상호 없음.

cards.title: Start with the harder side
body: Every marketplace has one side that's harder to win. Build that side first, even if the other side is the one paying.
Two questions find it. **Which side is scarcer?** And which side, once present, makes the other show up on its own? Usually it's the same side. At the night market and the mall, it's the sellers.
cards.softwareNote: For app platforms, the hard side is usually developers, because people pick a device or tool for what it can run. That's why platforms often court developers with tools, money and support before chasing users.

cards.title: Three ways to win the hard side.
body: Winning the scarce side takes effort. Most businesses use one of these:
list: **Pay for it:** rent discounts, a free first month, guaranteed income
**Give a tool useful on its own:** OpenTable gave restaurants reservation software that helped them even before many diners booked online
**Be the supply yourself:** do the work by hand until real sellers join
cards.callout: The cost is real. Treat it as an investment in the side that pulls everyone else in.
cards.softwareNote: The "useful tool" route suits software well: a free scheduling or invoicing tool can sign up the hard side long before the marketplace has buyers.

cards.title: Sometimes the buyers are the hard side.
body: Picture a house-cleaning marketplace in a city where many cleaners want more hours. Cleaners are easy to sign. Steady customers are scarce.
Here, lining up 200 cleaners with no jobs only teaches them the platform doesn't work. The smart move is to find customers first, perhaps through landlords or office managers.
The rule isn't "supply first." It's **scarce side first**.

cards.title: Don't make the first side wait.
body: The side you win first is paying with money, time or patience. If the other side doesn't arrive soon, they leave, and they tell others.
So keep the first side small and focused: one neighborhood, one category. That lets you bring in the other side quickly.
And the hard side can change. Once the night market's stalls are full, shoppers become the limit.

cards.title: Now it's a photographer booking app.
body: Your app books photographers for small events like birthdays and product shoots. In your city, hundreds of skilled part-time photographers want paid gigs. People hosting events rarely think to book one.
Where do you start?

options.text: Sign up 300 photographers so the app looks full
options.feedback: Easy to do, but most will get no bookings and drift away. A full-looking app with silent phones hurts trust on both sides.

options.text: Win clients first, through venues and party planners who host events
options.feedback: Clients are the scarce side here. Once real bookings flow, photographers will join with little push.

options.text: Sign 20 top photographers first, then work on clients
options.feedback: Quality helps your reputation, but photographers weren't the bottleneck. Keep that group small and put most effort into clients.

cards.title: Build the side that's hardest to get.
body: Ask which side is scarcer and which one pulls the other in. Spend there first, and keep it small enough that the other side arrives quickly.
**Try it today:** name the two sides of anything you run that connects people, such as suppliers and buyers or partners and clients. Which side would you struggle to find more of?
